title: How to fill PIQ form SSB
author: Defence Roger
data: Complete guide to filling out the Personal Information Questionnaire (PIQ) for NDA and SSB.
excerpt: Learn how to properly complete each of the 14 sections in the SSB PIQ form with practical advice on detailing your education, sports, hobbies, and family background without cluttering your form or making wrong entries.

content.text: It looks quite complicated at the start, but filling out the Personal Information Questionnaire (PIQ) form is actually very straightforward. I have seen many students struggle with what to fill and what to leave out, and unfortunately, I have seen many capable candidates miss out on a recommendation simply because they filled out their PIQ poorly. To help you maximize your chances of selection, let's break down how to actually fill out the PIQ form properly, section by section.
Overview of Sections 1 to 5: Basic Details & Residence
There are about 14 sections in total on the PIQ form:

content: Section 1: Contains four fields. You only need to fill in your UPSC Roll Number; the remaining fields will be provided and must be filled at the selection center.
Section 4: Place details. This is case-specific data—look up the population figures for your current residence, maximum residence, and permanent residence, and fill them in accordingly.
Section 5: Basic personal demographic details across five obvious fields.

content.caption: Image 1: Filling out basic personal details and residence demographics.

content.text: Section 6: Family Details & Clean Formatting

Section 6 covers the education, occupation, and income details of your family members. Try your best to keep everything neat and clean inside the allocated boxes. The spaces provided are quite small, and clutter leaves a poor first impression on the assessing officer.

content.caption: Image 2: Keeping family educational and occupational entries neat.

content.text: Section 7: Educational Qualifications & Extra-Curriculars
This section covers your qualifications across four fields: Matriculation (10th), 10+2 (12th), Graduation, and Post-Graduation. This is where you mention your key achievements during those years.

Avoid listing achievements that are too generic or average. For example, simply writing 'participated in a school debate in 10th class' adds little value. Focus on actual accomplishments rather than mere participation. Use concise terms that immediately catch the interviewing officer's eye—nothing overly flashy, but solid and genuine.
In my case, I listed placing 2nd in an open district-level basketball tournament during 10th grade, and winning a Youth Parliament event at Inter-KV level in 12th grade.

If you do not have formal achievements in a particular phase, leaving a box empty is completely fine. It is far better to leave a space blank than to fill it with weak or exaggerated claims. If you have multiple achievements, select a maximum of two top-tier accomplishments per section and list the most impressive one first to avoid a messy form.

content.caption: Image 3: Documenting educational background and achievements.

content.text: Section 8 & 9: Physical Measurements & Family Income

Section 8 asks for your age, height, and weight. A lot of aspirants wonder if being shorter or taller impacts their selection. The honest answer is that it does not matter whether you are a seven-foot giant or five feet tall. What matters is your character, mindset, and physical fitness. Focus on what you can control rather than unchangeable physical traits.
Section 9 simply asks for your family income and occupation details.

content.alt: PIQ Form Physical Measurements and Income
content.caption: Image 4: Filling out physical characteristics and family economic background.

content.text: Section 10: NCC Background
In Section 10, simply fill in your NCC background details if applicable, specifying whether you hold an 'A', 'B', or 'C' certificate.
Section 11(a): Sports & Games Achievements

Section 11 is critical because it frequently serves as a major foundation for questions during the personal interview. The interviewing officer uses this section to evaluate your physical activity, team spirit, and competitive drive throughout your lifetime.

If you have an active athletic background, list genuine accomplishments where you have demonstrated performance. In my case, I included my basketball tournament win, participation in district-level volleyball, relay races, a 1st-place finish in an inter-unit 5km marathon, and chess competition results featuring an official 1400 Elo rating.
Never fake any information here or anywhere else on the PIQ form. If you list a sport, be prepared for in-depth technical questions regarding rules, field dimensions, or performance timings.

When asked questions you don't know—such as exact court dimensions—politely state that you do not know rather than guessing. You are not expected to be an encyclopedia, but you are expected to be completely honest.

content.caption: Image 6: Highlighting sports participation and athletic achievements.

content.text: Section 11(b): Hobbies and Interests

In Section 11(b), mention activities you pursue regularly and are genuinely passionate about. Avoid generic or superficial answers like 'casual gaming' or 'gully cricket'. Choose pursuits you actively engage in and understand thoroughly.

For instance, I mentioned swimming (since I knew all four strokes and had performed a 10m board jump) and programming/web development, as I had actually built functional web applications. If you list hobbies like book reading or gardening, ensure you have deep, authentic knowledge—such as recent authors or specific techniques—as officers will cross-examine you thoroughly.

content.caption: Image 7: Detailing authentic hobbies and personal interests.

content.text: Section 11(c) & Positions of Responsibility

Section 11(c) focuses on extra-curricular achievements. If you do not have an extensive sports background, this is where academic and co-curricular accomplishments can shine. Include activities like debates, Olympiads, Model United Nations (MUN), or Youth Parliament.

Focus on achievements rather than mere participation or listing general exam ranks like JEE scores. Following this, under the Positions of Responsibility section, list leadership roles such as School Prefect, Head Boy, or Sports Captain. Be ready to discuss the responsibilities you managed and what you learned from those roles.

content.alt: PIQ Form Extra Curriculars and Leadership
content.caption: Image 8: Documenting extra-curricular excellence and leadership roles.

content.text: Sections 12, 13 & 14: Previous Attempts & Final Details

Section 12 repeats basic verification details matching your initial application. Section 13 covers the total number of attempts given for the services, and Section 14 asks for specific details regarding previous SSB interviews.
If you are a repeater, be thoroughly prepared for questions regarding your previous SSB experience and the improvements you have made since your last attempt.

content.caption: Image 9: Recording service attempt details and previous SSB history.
